title: Dell Latitude E5250 — 19V input short, capacitor restoration, second RTC/boot-start state

source.source_verification: web article reviewed; embedded video identified by link, no video frame by frame analysis

research_context.selection_mode: illustrative retrospective case study, selected AFTER public repair outcome was already known

chronology.title: Dead machine, healthy unloaded adapter, protection trip
previously_known_observations: The Dell Latitude E5250 has no boot and does not charge.
The Dell adapter indicator goes out as soon as it is attached to this laptop; it comes back after unplugging.
The disconnected adapter output measures 19.9 V on the repairer's multimeter.

source_measurements.condition: DC voltage at accessible adapter plug, not connected to laptop

chronology.decision_prompt: Identify where to localize lost power without assuming the battery or external adapter is bad.

chronology.title: Input rail draws heavy current; removing port does not remove short
previously_known_observations: Original repair technician reports the board took 2.3 A from a bench supply nominally set to 19 V while observed voltage collapsed nearly to zero.
Technician removed the power connector and measured persistent short on the board-side main input rail.
A diode/short test showed multiple capacitors on the same rail sharing the apparent short; individual capacitor causality not yet isolated.

source_measurements.target: board supply reported output current under fault
source_measurements.condition: technician described bench supply nominally set to 19 V with output collapsed near zero; not an instruction to replicate

source_measurements.target: bench supply nominal setting (not measured on board)
source_measurements.condition: technician-reported supply setting during failed power injection; actual rail nearly zero

chronology.decision_prompt: Discriminate input-port failure from downstream main-rail short and avoid replacing every capacitor on a shared net.

chronology.title: Current-sense resistor was misleading; shorted capacitor localized
previously_known_observations: During the technician's localization, a current-sense resistor first appeared hot because fault current was passing through it; that was a false localization.
After changing the injection location the repairer observed a particular ceramic capacitor heating; the short disappeared after that capacitor was removed.
The replacement part electrical value, dielectric, voltage rating, polarity-equivalence/footprint and exact board coordinates were not documented in the article.

source_measurements.condition: first injection position as reported; NOT an operating setpoint

chronology.decision_prompt: Stop at an isolated faulty part hypothesis until exact replacement specification and safety are verified.

chronology.title: Source technician replaced capacitor, but board still would not boot
previously_known_observations: The source technician fitted a ceramic capacitor harvested from an older MacBook donor board; capacitance, working voltage, dielectric and layout equivalence are not documented.
The board power rail later sat at 19.9 V and idle current reportedly dropped to around 40 mA.
The laptop still did not initially boot after partial reassembly despite 3.3 V being present on the power-button circuit and the 19.9 V input rail.

source_measurements.condition: after short removal, repair technician report; not a full machine idle current certification

source_measurements.target: board input rail after capacitor replacement

source_measurements.condition: board still failed to boot, source reported

chronology.decision_prompt: Re-open diagnosis for a second no-boot condition, rather than claiming complete repair because the input rail recovered.

chronology.title: Second boot issue attributed to BIOS/RTC battery startup state
previously_known_observations: The technician found that the laptop would start once the RTC/BIOS battery was disconnected before charger connection.
The technician described reconnecting the BIOS battery while the computer was powered, after which ordinary on/off cycling reportedly resumed.
HS does not authorize reconnecting an RTC battery to a powered board, and the article does not establish a permanent model-specific root cause for this state dependence.
chronology.decision_prompt: Record the second state-dependent boot blocker and require qualified safe diagnosis rather than hot-connecting the RTC battery.

chronology.title: Source reports OS-level functional boot and reassembly
previously_known_observations: The owner repair technician reports the machine booted to a Windows BitLocker recovery/unlock prompt on its existing encrypted drive.
The source reports repeated power on/off behavior was restored and mechanical reassembly completed.
No independently logged complete charge/discharge cycle, battery capacity test, long-duration thermal validation, post-repair data access, or customer signoff is supplied.
chronology.decision_prompt: Do not equate seeing BitLocker unlock screen with customer-grade full repair acceptance.

source_reported_interventions.action: Board voltage/current fault investigation with bench power and disassembly
Source used a flammable solvent heat/evaporation technique while sourcing a shorted element
Source removed failed MLCC, then fitted an unspecified old-MacBook donor MLCC
Source disconnected BIOS/RTC battery and later described reconnecting it on an energized board

conditional_bom.name: properly rated multimeter and probe accessories
current-limited bench supply and safe workholding (qualified technician only)
conditional_bom.source_verified_available: original technician used a bench supply

conditional_bom.name: non-contact thermal camera (preferred over any solvent heating method)
laptop main-input MLCC matching manufacturer board-level capacitor specification
Dell Latitude E5250 board revision specific repair manual / boardview
